card.hook: Picture marble figures in the foreground and the whole Detroit skyline standing up behind them, all on an island in the river. That's the James Scott Memorial Fountain, and it's the best first stop at Belle Isle.
card.stand_here: Walk to the James Scott Memorial Fountain and stand in front of it, then turn around to face the downtown skyline. If the plaza is closed when you visit, use the nearest open spot outside the closed area.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fountain with the skyline behind it. Try 0.5x from low down for the whole fountain and more sky, or 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to bring the skyline closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain on one side and the skyline along the upper line, then tap the bright part of the sky and drag a little darker so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunset is the favourite hour, when the sun is low and the skyline glows. Once the light fades, switch to night mode and rest your phone against a wall or railing.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on the James Scott Memorial Fountain plaza with the fountain's marble basin behind you, using the front camera. For more skyline, Sunset Point on the island's west-facing shore has the river and city in view, so hold your phone a little low and keep the city over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back in front of the Anna Scripps Whitcomb Conservatory so they can fit the full dome and building in the frame, while you stand on the grounds right in front of the dome.
card.rules_and_safety: Drivers need a Michigan Recreation Passport for their vehicle. Personal snapshots don't need a permit, but paid or commercial photo sessions do. The fountain isn't running until spring 2027 and work is under way, so check the official site for what's open before you go.
card.challenge: Get the fountain on one side and the skyline along the top gridline, with the horizon dead level. No wonky city allowed.
card.good_to_know: Belle Isle Park is a 982-acre island in the Detroit River, reached by the MacArthur Bridge. Frederick Law Olmsted, who designed New York's Central Park, was hired in the 1880s to plan it, though only some of his design was finished. Cass Gilbert designed the fountain, which was completed in 1925, and Albert Kahn designed the island's aquarium and conservatory.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the James Scott Memorial Fountain and stand in front of it, then turn around to face the downtown skyline. If the plaza is closed when you visit, use the nearest open spot outside the closed area.

card.hook: The best Eastern Market photo isn't in the busy sheds at all. It's down in a sunken path where cyclists and skaters whizz past a wall of murals.
card.stand_here: Stand at the northern end of the Dequindre Cut Greenway, next to Eastern Market. The market sheds are about 240 m to the south-west of you. Face the mural wall, and if you can get onto a bridge above the cut, shoot down onto the wall and the path.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get riders and mural together, then try 0.5x to squeeze in the whole painted wall and the cut below. To pick out a single rider, go to zoom 2x-5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the rider's path, then slide the brightness a little darker so the mural colours stay rich and the bright sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, when the light falls into the cut at an angle. If you want the market sheds instead, go early on a Saturday, but expect crowds.
card.selfie_here: Try the "Checkered Past" checkerboard mural at 2520 Orleans St, a short walk from Shed 5 and Bert's Warehouse. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x for more wall, and let the mural fill the space behind you. The sheds won't be in the shot, so think of this one as a colourful street-art selfie.
card.rules_and_safety: Vendors are usually happy to be photographed if you buy something and ask first. Photos of people in public are generally legal, but using a recognisable person's image commercially needs their release. On market days (Tuesday and Saturday) street parking is limited, and the Russell Street parking structure is the safer bet.
card.challenge: Catch a cyclist crossing the mural just as their jacket matches a colour on the wall, and give yourself a point if you do it in one try.
card.good_to_know: Eastern Market is a working market district, so it's a lively, very local place. The Dequindre Cut Greenway runs sunken below street level, and its walls are covered in murals. If the sheds feel crowded, Lincoln Street Art Park nearby is a quieter spot for street art, and the Aretha Franklin mural at Winder St and Russell St is another colourful corner. Murals rotate, so some walls may look different from older guides.

card.hook: Ford Field is about 390 m across on our map, so the real trick here isn't finding it, it's fitting it all in your frame. Let the road do some of the work for you.
card.stand_here: Stand on the pavement on Brush Street, on the stretch across from Comerica Park. Ford Field is to the north-east, on one side of the street, so face that way and let the road lead your eye along its front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the street view. If the stadium front won't fit, switch to 0.5x, and use 2x when you want to pick out a detail like the marquee.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the road up with them, and tap the stadium wall; if the sky looks washed out, slide it a little darker.
card.best_time: Pick a day with no Lions game or event, in daylight, when the street is quieter and easier to shoot. Check the stadium's event calendar before you go.
card.selfie_here: Try the sidewalk in front of the glass atrium on the Brush Street side, with the building behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the stadium over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Comerica Park side of Brush Street, facing Ford Field so the whole stadium fits, while you pose on the sidewalk in front of the atrium.
card.rules_and_safety: Brush Street is closed on Lions game days for the pregame gathering, and entry to the stadium is ticketed. Selfie sticks are prohibited at Ford Field stadium events.
card.challenge: Can you get the road, the stadium and your own grin all in one shot, with the building edges dead straight?
card.good_to_know: The stadium was built around an old Hudson's warehouse from the 1920s, which is now offices. The playing field is sunk 45 feet (14 m) below street level, and the frosted windows near the roofline echo Detroit's car factories. Super Bowl XL was played here on 5 February 2006.

card.hook: Picture a museum made entirely of white marble, sitting calm and perfectly balanced against the sky. That's the Detroit Institute of Arts, and it's wide enough that your phone will need a little help.
card.stand_here: Stand about 25 m west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face east towards the Detroit Institute of Arts. If the whole width won't fit, take a few steps back rather than tilting the phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so both wings and the middle block fit in one frame. Then switch to 1x for a more natural view, or 2x to pick out the marble detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof edge with a horizontal line so the building doesn't look like it's leaning.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light suits white marble best. Midday glare can wash it out into one big white patch, so tap the building and slide the brightness a touch darker if that happens.
card.selfie_here: Head to the white marble front staircase on the Woodward Avenue side and stand a step or two up, so the museum rises behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and hold it slightly low so the building fits over your shoulder. The wrought-iron gates at the Woodward entrance make a good backup backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across Woodward Avenue in front of the main branch of the Detroit Public Library, while you pose on the steps, so they can frame the whole museum front behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside the museum can differ from outside, so check the official site before you go. Outside, keep clear of the entrance so visitors can get past.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the roofline is dead straight on a gridline, and your hat or hair is the only thing that isn't perfectly symmetrical.
card.good_to_know: The DIA is one of the largest art museums in the United States, with over 100 galleries and more than 65,000 works. The original building was designed by Paul Philippe Cret, and the museum's first painting was donated in 1883. Inside, Diego Rivera's Detroit Industry frescoes surround the central grand court.

card.hook: You could walk right past this little house and never guess that it launched a whole sound. That gap between ordinary and extraordinary is exactly why it's fun to photograph.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sidewalk on West Grand Boulevard (it's also signed Berry Gordy Jr. Boulevard here), with the museum 50 m to the east. Face east so the brick front and the Motown sign are right ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole house in its street. Then try 2x for a tighter shot of the front. Use 0.5x only if you've stepped closer and the frontage won't fit.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the house's upright edges up with them so the walls don't lean, and hold your phone level at chest height instead of tilting it up.
card.best_time: A bright overcast day gives soft, even light that suits the house well. On a sunny day, afternoon light should be behind you as you look east, but check that nothing is shading the front.
card.selfie_here: Climb up to the steps of the Hitsville U.S.A. house at 2648 West Grand Boulevard and put the building behind you, or stand on the sidewalk in front of the blue-and-white Hitsville U.S.A. sign. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and hold it a little low so the sign and facade stay over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Check opening and construction access before you go, as the museum may be closed for building work. Photography is generally allowed inside, but follow the guide and any signs, and avoid flash in certain areas.
card.challenge: Get two shots: one wide with a bit of street in the foreground, and one close on the front. Can you keep both sets of walls dead straight against the gridlines?
card.good_to_know: Berry Gordy bought the house in 1959 and turned the back of the old photographers' studio into a recording room. His family lived upstairs at first, and within a few years the label had taken over several neighbouring houses. Today the museum fills the original house plus an adjacent former residence, and Studio A is kept as it was, with an 1877 Steinway grand piano.

card.hook: Most ballparks hide behind parking and concrete. This one sits right in the middle of downtown, so the trick is to photograph it as part of the city, not as a lonely building.
card.stand_here: Stand in Grand Circus Park and approach from the Woodward Avenue side, where the ballpark comes into view across a parking lot. The ballpark is to the north-east, so face that way and let the green space and paved walks lead the eye to the stadium.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wide view of the park with the ballpark beyond. Try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick the stadium out from a distance, and save zoom 0.5x for the tiger statue up close.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the path or lawn in the lower third and the stadium on one of the upper lines, then tap the stadium and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Daytime gives you the clearest view of the stadium from the park. Early evening can add warmer light and a livelier feel.
card.selfie_here: Head to the main A gate and stand on the ground-level sidewalk beside the 15-foot tiger statue, which fans line up to pose with. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and let the big cat loom next to you.
card.ask_someone: Stand in Grand Circus Park, across the parking lot from the ballpark, and ask a passer-by to take your photo with the stadium in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the ballpark, though phones are fine. Game days bring crowds and possible closures, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find one of the tiger heads on the brick walls outside and get its lit-up baseball in your shot.
card.good_to_know: Comerica Park opened in 2000 in a retro-classic style and seats 41,083 people. Eight more big tiger statues are inside, and 33 tiger heads with lit-up baseballs in their mouths line the outside brick walls. The stadium is expected to be renamed Fifth Third Park before the 2027 season, so signs may change.

card.hook: Most towers make you crane your neck. The Fisher Building's roof does the work for you: a green-tiled crown that glows gold after dark. Everyone looks up, so get your phone up too.
card.stand_here: Stand at Cadillac Place, at the entrance portico across West Grand Boulevard from the Fisher Building. Face north-west and the tower rises over the street, with the neighbouring Kahn-designed building framing one side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the tower, the street and the neighbouring building in one shot. Tap 2x for a tighter picture of the roof and upper floors. Zoom 0.5x fits the whole tower in if you're close.
card.make_it_pop: Hold the phone upright, switch on the gridlines, and line the tower up with a vertical grid line, leaving a little sky above the roof.
card.best_time: Go at dusk or in the evening, when the roof is lit and looks golden. In daylight, the facade is easier to read when the sun isn't straight in your lens.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the West Grand Boulevard sidewalk in front of the main arched entrance, so the Art Deco facade rises behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more of the building in, and keep the landmark over your shoulder. Want a different backdrop? Step just inside the entrance hallway for a pic under the vaulted ceiling.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk in front of Cadillac Place, across West Grand Boulevard, while you pose by the Fisher so the tower fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Exterior views from public sidewalks are fine, but the Cadillac Place portico depends on current access, so check before you go. For photos inside, rules vary between reports, so check with the building (313.874.1100) first.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead straight on a grid line with a sliver of sky above the roof, then do it again at dusk and see which one wins.
card.good_to_know: The Fisher Building is a 30-storey Art Deco tower finished in 1928 and designed by Albert Kahn's firm. It stands 428 feet (130 m) to the roof and has been called "Detroit's largest art object". The roof tiles were first gold leaf, later replaced with green ones, and coloured lights have made them look golden at night since the 1980s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Cadillac Place, at the entrance portico across West Grand Boulevard from the Fisher Building. Face north-west and the tower rises over the street, with the neighbouring Kahn-designed building framing one side.

card.hook: Picture beach-style seating on a lawn in the middle of downtown, with a ring of tall towers standing around like an audience. Come back in winter and the same spot has a holiday tree and an ice rink instead.
card.stand_here: Stand on the lawn near the Woodward Fountain (the phone icon on the map marks the spot) and look across the park. Put the fountain low in the frame and let the towers fill the background.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the lawn, fountain and towers all in one shot. Drop to 0.5x if the park is busy and you need to stand close, or if you want more skyline. Use zoom 2x for details like the fountain spray.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the fountain on a lower line with the towers in the top third, and keep your phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Pick your season. Summer gives you the beach-style seating, and winter gives you the tree and the rink. The setups change, so check what's on before you go. On winter evenings, try night mode and hold your phone steady against your body to catch the tree lights.
card.selfie_here: Try Woodward Avenue, facing north, with the park right behind you. It's near the 800 Woodward Ave entrance. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the park and city fit over your shoulder. It's only a suggestion from a photo guide, so check the spot on site.
card.rules_and_safety: Private security patrols the area, so keep your kit simple and just use your phone. Events and seasonal attractions like the rink may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the medallion set into the stone walkway at the western point of the diamond around the fountain, and get a close-up at zoom 2x.
card.good_to_know: The park was dedicated on 19 November 2004 and covers 1.2 acres. It re-creates an older square that was lost when downtown was reshaped for traffic. The medallion in the walkway is the point of origin of Detroit's coordinate system, and the Michigan Soldiers' and Sailors' Monument, a Civil War-era memorial, is nearby if you want another subject.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the lawn near the Woodward Fountain (the phone icon on the map marks the spot) and look across the park. Put the fountain low in the frame and let the towers fill the background.

card.hook: Picture a long path hugging open water, the city stacked up behind it, and a row of people leaning on the railing as the sun goes down. That's the Detroit Riverwalk, and it's even better than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand at the riverfront edge of Hart Plaza, right where the Riverwalk begins next to the Renaissance Center. Face along the path so it runs away beside the water, with the skyline and the Windsor shoreline behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the river, the skyline and the far shore. Move closer to the Renaissance Center and switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the towers in. At zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone), you can pick out people leaning on the railing.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the railing along a lower line so the path leads the eye along the river, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when people line the rail with the river and skyline behind them. Tap the skyline, then slide to a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.selfie_here: Try Hart Plaza, in front of the Horace E. Dodge Fountain. Visitor reviews describe posing here with the city and Windsor across the river, and one calls it a signature Detroit photo spot. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more, and keep the view over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by near the Cullen Plaza stretch of the Riverwalk to take your photo, and have them frame the path and the skyline together.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual personal photos along the Detroit Riverfront don't need a permit, but don't block the pathways. A travel guide says the Riverwalk is well-lit at night. Events and festivals are held on the riverfront, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a stranger leaning on the railing at the edge of your frame, so your sunset shot has a bit of life in it. Bonus points for a perfectly level horizon.
card.good_to_know: The Riverwalk is part of the Detroit International Riverfront, which stretches 5.5 miles from the Ambassador Bridge to Belle Isle. USA Today readers voted it the best riverwalk in the United States in 2021, 2022 and 2023. The Renaissance Center is seven linked towers and has been the tallest building in Michigan since 1977.

card.hook: Most people hurry inside for the famous lobby, but the outside of the Guardian Building is the real show. It's a tower of warm orange brick, tile and terra cotta set in bold geometric patterns, right in the middle of downtown Detroit.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Griswold Street and Congress Street, diagonally across the intersection from the building's corner, with the building to the south-east. Face it and you'll see the orange north face, its huge arched window with the coloured tile surround, and the whole tower climbing above.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full height and the big arched window in one shot. Then try 1x for a more natural look at the north face, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to home in on the tile and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brick, then slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out and the orange stays rich.
card.best_time: Bright daylight shows off the brick and tile colours best. Avoid very harsh midday sun, which can make the stonework look flat.
card.selfie_here: Try the Griswold Street pavement by the main entrance (500 Griswold St), where you can see the taller north tower. Use the front camera, hold it a little low, and let the tower rise over your shoulder (0.5x helps if your phone has it). Campus Martius Park is a good backup for a wider backdrop of the tower.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from Woodward Avenue just north of Jefferson Avenue, by the Spirit of Detroit sculpture, with you in the frame, so both towers fit in the photo.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside is fine to photograph from the public pavement. It's an office building, so check the official site before you go if you want to head inside, where photos are generally fine without flash.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, keep the phone upright, and put the arched window in the lower-middle so the tower shoots straight up out of it. Bonus points if you can keep the traffic out.
card.good_to_know: The 43-story tower was built in 1928-29 as the Union Trust Building, and it's nicknamed the Cathedral of Finance. Two sculptures by Corrado Parducci flank the Griswold Street entrance. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1989 and is now owned by Wayne County.

card.hook: For years this was the ruin everyone in Detroit pointed at, and the last trains left in January 1988. Now you can stroll across a lawn and snap it looking like a movie poster.
card.stand_here: Stand in Roosevelt Park, on the front (north) side of the station, across the park paths. The building is directly south of you, so face south toward the main facade and entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade, tower and lawns in one go. Switch to zoom 2x to pick out the tower and the carved stonework. Use zoom 0.5x only if you walk closer and want the full height of the building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the entrance on the centre line and keep your phone level so the tower stands up straight.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, when the light hits the windows and the weathered stone. Summer weekends can be busy, so go earlier if you want fewer people in the frame.
card.selfie_here: Head to the park lawn directly out front and turn your back to the station's main facade. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the whole building rises up over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by in the park out front, then stand in the foreground with the station's facade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Roosevelt Park is a free public park. Check the official site before you go for station access, event closures and any rules for photography inside.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly upright with the entrance dead centre, and a park path leading your eye straight to the door.
card.good_to_know: Michigan Central Station was finished in 1913-14, and it was the tallest railway station in the world when it was built. Its office tower is 230 feet (70 m) tall. Ford bought it in 2018, and after a restoration costing more than $900 million it reopened on 6 June 2024.

card.hook: One fat round tower, ringed by smaller ones, all glass, all shouting 'look at me' across the Detroit riverfront. Locals call it the RenCen, and it's the easiest skyline to spot in town.
card.stand_here: Go to the spot near Atwater Street, at the phone icon on the map, about 110 m south of the numbered pin. Face north and the towers rise right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the tall middle tower and its neighbours into one frame. Then switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look. At 0.5x, keep people and objects away from the edges, where they get stretched.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up one tower edge with a grid line, and hold the phone level so the sides stay straight.
card.best_time: Late morning to mid-afternoon can light up the glass facing you. Around sunset the glass can pick up warm colour, and just after dusk night mode can catch the lit towers against a deep blue sky. For night shots, rest your phone against something solid to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the Detroit RiverWalk edge beside the Renaissance Center, which one blog recommends for dusk and night shots with the towers and their reflections in the frame. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if you can) and keep the towers over your shoulder. Hart Plaza is another option, with the RenCen in the skyline view behind you.
card.ask_someone: At Hart Plaza, ask a passer-by to stand on the plaza and frame you with the RenCen in view across the riverfront.
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the buildings and plaza may change as the site is redeveloped, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the round tower in one shot with a bit of sky above it so it doesn't look 'decapitated', then crouch for a second shot with something in the foreground.
card.good_to_know: The RenCen has seven connected towers. The tallest is the round 74-storey hotel in the middle, the tallest building in Michigan. Architect John Portman designed it in the 1970s as a 'city-within-a-city'. General Motors moved its headquarters out in early 2026, and part of the site is planned for demolition and redevelopment, so the view may look different from older photos.

card.hook: Picture a ten-storey cream tower with Asian-inspired decoration, and a glowing marquee parked right at its feet. The Fox doesn't whisper, so don't be shy about it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Woodward Avenue corner, where the two streets meet, with the theatre a very short distance to the south. Face south so you're looking straight at the front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tall façade and the marquee in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the marquee lettering and the terracotta decoration.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the marquee, then slide to darker just a touch so the neon doesn't wash out to white.
card.best_time: Evening is the showstopper, when the façade and marquee are lit up. In daylight, the cream terracotta and its fine detail look best.
card.selfie_here: Try the Comerica Park side, standing directly beneath the marquee, since that's the one spot we know looks up at it. Use the front camera, tilt up a little and let the marquee sit over your shoulder, and check on the spot that it works.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite side of Woodward Avenue, facing the marquee and main entrance, while you pose near the entrance so the whole front fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos aren't allowed in the side areas of the theatre or backstage, and videography isn't permitted. Some shows don't allow photography once they start, so get your pictures early.
card.challenge: Catch the tall tower, the marquee and one passing car in a single frame, and give yourself bonus points if the building stands up straight.
card.good_to_know: The Fox opened in 1928 as a flagship movie palace, designed by C. Howard Crane. With 5,048 seats, it's the largest surviving movie palace of the 1920s. It was fully restored in 1988 and became a National Historic Landmark in 1989.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Woodward Avenue corner, where the two streets meet, with the theatre a very short distance to the south. Face south so you're looking straight at the front.

card.hook: Good luck getting the whole Detroit Opera House into one photo from the front steps. It's a big, decorated building, and it just keeps going.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near Broadway Street, about 20 m south of the numbered pin, and face north. Stay on the pavement and out of the road.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long front in from close up. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details higher up.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so it doesn't lean, and hold your phone upright rather than tilted up.
card.best_time: Daylight is easiest if you want to see the stonework and details. Dusk or early evening is lovely for lit signs and warm light, so let night mode do its thing and hold the phone still against your body.
card.selfie_here: Try the southwest corner at John R and Broadway, where the huge proscenium mural is visible. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and keep the building over your shoulder. If you're going inside, the main staircase off the Broadway lobby is a lovely backdrop too.

card.rules_and_safety: Photos and video are generally not allowed during performances, but lobby and common areas are usually fine before the show or at intermission. Check the official site before you go if you want to see inside.
card.challenge: Take three close-ups: some sign lettering, a doorway and a bit of decorative stonework. Bonus points if nobody walks through the shot.
card.good_to_know: The building opened on 22 January 1922 as the Capitol Theatre, designed by C. Howard Crane. After closures in 1978 and 1985, the Michigan Opera Theatre bought it in 1988. It reopened in 1996 as the Detroit Opera House and now seats 2,700.

card.hook: Hart Plaza after dark is a bit of a show-off: the fountain lights up, the jets leap, and the whole downtown skyline stands behind them like an audience.
card.stand_here: Head for the Horace E. Dodge Fountain in the middle of the plaza and stand at the fountain's edge. Face the water jets, so the downtown skyline rises behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the jets and the skyline in one frame. Try 1x for a calmer view with less stretching at the edges. Then try zoom 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out a single jet.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest jets, then slide the brightness down a little so the lit water doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the fountain is lit up. Use night mode and tuck your elbows against your body to keep the phone still.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the Horace E. Dodge Fountain, use the front camera at 0.5x, and let the fountain and its lit-up water fill the background over your shoulder. For a second option, pose at the bronze Fist on Jefferson Avenue with the plaza grounds behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from the fountain, with you in front of it, so the basin and the downtown skyline fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Summer festivals can fence off or crowd parts of the plaza, so check the official site before you go and be flexible about where you stand. The atmosphere can vary with the event and the crowd it draws.
card.challenge: Switch on Live Photo and try to catch a jet at its highest, then scroll through afterwards and pick your best frame.
card.good_to_know: Hart Plaza opened in 1975 and can hold about 40,000 people for concerts and festivals. It sits roughly where Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac landed in 1701 to found the settlement that became Detroit. The Dodge fountain was designed by Isamu Noguchi and Walter Budd in 1978.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Horace E. Dodge Fountain in the middle of the plaza and stand at the fountain's edge. Face the water jets, so the downtown skyline rises behind them.

card.hook: A 26-foot bronze giant sits in front of a white marble wall, holding a golden sphere in one hand and a tiny family in the other. Yes, he's as photogenic as he sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, on Spirit Plaza in front of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center, and face the statue head-on. The statue is to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic front view. Switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole statue, the curved marble wall and some of the plaza in one shot. Zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) gets you close to the golden sphere and the little family.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bronze figure, then slide the brightness down a touch so the white marble doesn't glare.
card.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon are suggested for the best light. It's a popular portrait spot, so you may need to wait a moment for a clear shot.
card.selfie_here: Take it on Spirit Plaza, directly in front of the statue, which is where visitors get their classic shots. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt it so the bronze figure towers over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few steps back on Spirit Plaza while you stand in front of the statue, so the full 26-foot figure fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Spirit Plaza and the statue are free and open to the public.
card.challenge: Copy the statue's pose in your photo, one arm out holding your own 'golden sphere' (a coffee cup counts).
card.good_to_know: Marshall Fredericks made the Spirit of Detroit, and it was dedicated in 1958. At about 26 feet (7.9 m) tall, it's one of the largest bronze statues in the United States. During big city events it's sometimes dressed in oversized team jerseys, so your photo might look different from the one you planned.

card.hook: Picture a 45-storey limestone tower stepping up into the sky like a stack of wedding-cake tiers, with a red beacon on top as the cherry. That's the Penobscot, and it towers over Detroit's Campus Martius Park like it owns the place.
card.stand_here: Stand in Campus Martius Park and face south-west. The Penobscot Building is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot, so look for the stepped tower with the red beacon.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, the park and the whole tower in one frame. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the stepped top and the beacon.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky just above the tower's top, then drag the slider down so the picture gets a little darker and the limestone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon and stay into dusk. The tower is lit at night, and on holidays the lights change colour. At Christmas the broadcast tower glows gold.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Campus Martius Park, anywhere you can see the tower rising behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and tilt up just a little so the tower sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the corner of Griswold Street and West Fort Street, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to frame the whole tower and its neighbours with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: The Penobscot is a private office block, so keep your photos to the outside and the park.
card.challenge: Get the fountain in the bottom third and the red beacon at the very top of the same shot, then check whether the tower's sides stayed straight.
card.good_to_know: The Penobscot Building went up between 1927 and 1928 and stands 566 feet (173 m) tall. It was the tallest building in Detroit and in Michigan until 1977. Architect Wirt C. Rowland clad it in Indiana limestone.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Campus Martius Park and face south-west. The Penobscot Building is to the south-west, about 3 minutes on foot, so look for the stepped tower with the red beacon.

card.hook: Picture a bronze fist the size of a small bus, hanging in the middle of one of downtown Detroit's busiest junctions. Somehow it still looks like it's about to bump yours.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Woodward Avenue and Jefferson Avenue, on the side across the street from the monument. The monument is to the north-west of you, so face north-west and you'll see the arm and pyramid frame head-on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the fist and frame head-on. Go to 0.5x for the whole frame with more of the downtown towers, or 2x to pick out the knuckles.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bronze, then slide it a touch darker so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Sunrise or sunset is best. The sculpture is lit at night too, so try night mode and lean the phone against a post or your body to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Hart Plaza side of the monument, where you can stand at the base with the arm rising behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and tuck the arm and pyramid frame over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the street facing the arm and step back until the whole pyramid frame fits, while you pose by the fist, but only if you can reach it safely.
card.rules_and_safety: Traffic is busy here, so take your photos from the pavement and cross only at the crossings.
card.challenge: Pose with your own fist out, like you're about to bump the giant one, and get a friend to capture the moment just before impact.
card.good_to_know: The Monument to Joe Louis, nicknamed The Fist, was made by sculptor Robert Graham and given by Sports Illustrated. It was dedicated on 16 October 1986. The arm is 24 feet (7.3 m) long, and it points towards Canada, which is said to be deliberate.

card.hook: Picture a half-moon of green in the middle of downtown Detroit, with a fountain in each half and tall buildings leaning in over the trees. Woodward Avenue cuts straight through it, so you get two parks for the price of one.
card.stand_here: Stand near Witherell Street, about 40 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. That puts the fountain in front of you with the trees and buildings behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fountain and its surroundings. Switch to 0.5x when you want the fountain, the trees and the tall buildings all in one frame, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the statues or the tops of the buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the fountain on one of the lower lines, and hold your phone low and level so the buildings stay upright.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the tall buildings throw less harsh shade across the park. Weekday midday tends to be busier with people.
card.selfie_here: Take it in front of the Russell A. Alger Memorial Fountain at the centre of the park, ideally in morning light. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a bit low so the fountain and the historic buildings fit over your shoulder. The Detroit sign inside the park is another popular snapshot spot.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one with a fountain and a building in the same frame, and one that's just open greenery. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: The city established the park in 1850 as part of Augustus Woodward's plan to rebuild after the 1805 fire. The original idea was a full circle, but that was never finished. The Alger Fountain on the eastern half dates from 1921 and was designed by Henry Bacon, who also designed the Lincoln Memorial, while the western half has the Edison Fountain.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Witherell Street, about 40 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. That puts the fountain in front of you with the trees and buildings behind it.

card.hook: A bronze woman stands in the middle of Detroit with one hand raised, as if she's saying hello to you. The other hand holds a sword and shield, so she's friendly but not to be messed with.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, near Adams Avenue East, at the Russell Alger Memorial Fountain in Grand Circus Park. Face the fountain so the whole monument fits in your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole fountain in one shot. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the park around it, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for the raised hand, the shield and the lion heads.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bright sky, then slide it a little darker so the bronze figure keeps its detail instead of turning into a dark shape.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the bronze and granite better than harsh midday sun. Pick a moment when the water's flowing so you get a lively foreground.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the fountain itself, on the east side of Grand Circus Park at the corner of East Adams Street and Woodward Avenue. A travel guide calls it a prime photo spot and suggests morning light, so use the front camera (try 0.5x) and keep the statue over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the path leading up to the fountain, while you stand near the fountain so they can fit you, the statue and the basin in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Check local information before you go for any works or closures.
card.challenge: Can you line up her raised hand so it looks like she's waving at the camera, or at you?
card.good_to_know: The fountain was dedicated on 27 July 1921 and was made by sculptor Daniel Chester French, architect Henry Bacon and the Gorham Manufacturing Company. The figure represents Michigan, and the shield carries the state crest. It honours Russell Alger, who rose from private to general in the Civil War, then became Governor of Michigan, a U.S. Senator and U.S. Secretary of War. A society of Civil War veterans commissioned it in his memory.
